exceedance.source: Climate Action Tracker Nov 2026 percentiles; WMO 2025
exceedance.reasoning: Warming was already 1.43 °C in 2025 and even CAT's 16th percentile for 2100 is 2.2 °C, so ending the century below 1.2 °C is essentially ruled out.

exceedance.source: Climate Action Tracker Nov 2026; Liu & Raftery 2021
exceedance.reasoning: A two-piece normal fitted to CAT's published 16th/50th/84th percentiles (2.2/2.7/3.4 °C) gives 0.99, and Liu & Raftery publish a below-2% chance of staying under 1.5 °C.

exceedance.source: Climate Action Tracker Nov 2026
exceedance.reasoning: Same CAT fit gives 0.92; cross-checks: Liu & Raftery publish 0.95, IPCC SSP2-4.5 implies 0.97, a fit to UNEP's 66th/90th percentiles about 0.77.

exceedance.source: Climate Action Tracker Nov 2026
exceedance.reasoning: CAT fit gives 0.66; cross-checks span 0.51 (UNEP fit) to 0.76 (Liu & Raftery fit), with IPCC SSP2-4.5 at 0.71.

exceedance.source: Climate Action Tracker Nov 2026
exceedance.reasoning: CAT's 66th percentile is exactly 3.0 °C, so 0.34 is published; cross-checks: UNEP fit 0.24, IPCC SSP2-4.5 0.27, Liu & Raftery fit 0.38.

exceedance.source: Climate Action Tracker Nov 2026; UNEP EGR 2026
exceedance.reasoning: CAT fit gives 0.13 and CAT publishes 0.16 above 3.4 °C; UNEP publishes 0.10 above 3.4 °C, so 3.5 °C sits near 0.08-0.13.

exceedance.source: Climate Action Tracker Nov 2026
exceedance.reasoning: CAT fit gives 0.03 (UNEP fit 0.02, Liu & Raftery fit 0.04); this tail ignores the chance that policies weaken, which would fatten it.

exceedance.source: Jiang et al. 2023 / Meinshausen et al. 2020 SSP concentrations
exceedance.reasoning: Even the lowest IPCC pathway (SSP1-1.9) ends the century at 393 ppm, so every assessed path stays above 350 ppm in 2100.

exceedance.source: Judgment from SSP concentrations and CAT scenarios
exceedance.reasoning: Only paths at or below SSP1-2.6 (446 ppm in 2100, about CAT's optimistic 1.9 °C case with every net-zero pledge met) end below 450, and at today's 2-3.75 ppm/yr growth (NOAA) the world passes 450 ppm in the 2030s anyway.

exceedance.source: Findlay et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2023
exceedance.reasoning: This stricter line was passed around 2000 and even the lowest-emission pathway only recovers to 2.9 by 2100.

exceedance.source: Planetary Health Check 2026; Jiang et al. 2023
exceedance.reasoning: Already 2.85 in 2024; only an SSP1-1.9-type path (2.9 in 2100, CO2 back near 393 ppm) climbs back above the line, and UNEP now says limiting warming to 1.5 °C without overshoot has been lost.

exceedance.source: Derived carbonate chemistry from Jiang et al. 2023; CAT Nov 2026 scenarios
exceedance.reasoning: Saturation falls below 2.50 once atmospheric CO2 passes roughly 540-560 ppm (derived), which current policies (~SSP2-4.5, 603 ppm, ~2.35) exceed but full delivery of pledges (CAT 2.1 °C) would not.

exceedance.source: IPCC AR6 WG1 SSP2-4.5 distribution (56 cm, likely 44-76)
exceedance.reasoning: A two-piece normal fitted to AR6's SSP2-4.5 median and 17-83% range gives 0.68 above 50 cm (relative to 1995-2014); SSP1-2.6 would give 0.38 and SSP3-7.0 0.91.

exceedance.source: IPCC AR6 WG1; Bamber et al. 2019
exceedance.reasoning: AR6's medium-confidence SSP2-4.5 distribution implies about 0.02, raised to 0.05 for poorly understood ice-sheet processes (experts put a 95th-percentile ice-sheet contribution of 81 cm at +2 °C).

exceedance.source: Jahn 2018, Nature Climate Change; CAT Nov 2026 warming distribution
exceedance.reasoning: Jahn finds a 100% chance of at least one ice-free summer by 2100 at 2 °C and 30% at 1.5 °C; weighting by the CAT-derived warming odds (0.92 above 2 °C) gives about 0.97 for at least one ice-free September.

exceedance.source: IPCC AR6 WG1 Ch. 9 (25% per °C); CAT Nov 2026
exceedance.reasoning: At 25% per °C a 50% loss needs about 2.85 °C of warming (0.42 by the CAT fit), trimmed to 0.35 because frozen ground lags air temperature.

exceedance.source: IPCC AR6 WG1 Ch. 9; CAT Nov 2026
exceedance.reasoning: A 75% loss needs close to 3.85 °C by the 25%-per-°C rule (about 0.05 by the CAT fit), though AR6 says losses of up to 75% are possible at 2-3 °C.

exceedance.source: Judgment from Living Planet Report 2026 trend
exceedance.reasoning: Staying under 80% requires the index to fall less than 0.4% a year to 2100, about a sixth of the 1970-2022 average rate, while habitat loss and warming continue.

exceedance.source: Judgment from Living Planet Report 2026 trend
exceedance.reasoning: Reaching 90% needs about half the historical rate of decline sustained for 78 years, plausible but not the central case given conservation gains and index revisions.

exceedance.source: Judgment from Planetary Health Check 2026
exceedance.reasoning: Ozone is recovering and global aerosol loading is improving, so an eighth crossing would need a new shock such as large-scale stratospheric aerosol injection or an ozone-depleting surprise.

exceedance.source: Judgment from Planetary Health Check 2026
exceedance.reasoning: Requires both remaining boundaries to fail at once, which no current trend points to.

exceedance.source: Drijfhout et al. 2025; Portmann et al. 2026; Bonan et al. 2025
exceedance.reasoning: 37% of CMIP6 SSP2-4.5 runs fall below about 10 Sv by 2100; the newest observation-constrained estimate (about 51% weakening) points lower, another (18-43%) higher.

exceedance.source: IPCC AR6; Drijfhout et al. 2025; van Westen et al. 2024; Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen 2023; Cini et al. EGU26
exceedance.reasoning: A fully collapsed state by 2100 is unlikely because shutdown takes 50-100 years after tipping, but early-warning and CESM studies put tipping itself this century, so the chance is not small.

notes: WARMING PROBABILITIES: the primary numbers are derived from CAT's November 2026 current-policy distribution (16th 2.2, median 2.7, 66th 3.0, 84th 3.4 °C), fitted with a two-piece normal. Cross-check table (P above 1.5 / 2 / 2.5 / 3 / 3.5 / 4 °C): CAT 0.99/0.92/0.66/0.34/0.13/0.03; UNEP EGR 2026 fit (66th 2.8, 90th 3.4, assumed symmetric) 0.93/0.77/0.51/0.24/0.08/0.02; Liu & Raftery 2021 fit (5th 2.1, median 2.8, 95th 3.9) 1.00/0.97/0.76/0.38/0.15/0.04; IPCC SSP2-4.5 fit (2081-2100) 1.00/0.97/0.71/0.27/0.05/0.004; Raftery 2017 (older data) 0.99/0.95/0.83/0.61/0.39/0.22. Published points: CAT P(>2.7)=0.50, P(>3.0)=0.34, P(>3.4)=0.16; UNEP P(>2.8)=0.34, P(>3.4)=0.10; Liu & Raftery P(<2)=0.05, P(<1.5)<0.02.

WARMING CAVEATS: these distributions hold today's policies fixed. They do not include the chance that policy strengthens (CAT pledges case 2.1 °C, optimistic 1.9 °C) or weakens (rollbacks), nor a special SI effect. Temperatures keep rising after 2100 under current policies (CAT). Liu & Raftery use 1860-1880 as baseline; others use 1850-1900.

UNEP RANGE CONFLICT: Carbon Brief reports a 10% chance of exceeding 3.4 °C under current policies (10-90% box for a central emissions path). CAT's annex reports the EGR current-policy range as 1.6-4.5 °C, which appears to also include emissions-path uncertainty. The full EGR PDF could not be read (unep.org returns 403).

'BY 2100' MEANING: all exceedance values above refer to the end-of-century state (2100 value or 2081-2100 mean), not a temporary crossing. Under an 'at any point before 2100' reading: warming above 1.5 °C is ~1.0 (CAT: long-term crossing around 2030); CO2 above 450 ppm is ~1.0 (PHC put 2026 at 426 ppm and NOAA's growth was 2.03 ppm in 2025 and a record 3.75 in 2024, so 450 is reached in the 2030s); the Arctic value is already an 'at least once' probability.

OCEAN ACIDIFICATION 2100 VALUE IS DERIVED, NOT PUBLISHED: 2.35 (2.3-2.45) under SSP2-4.5 comes from a one-box carbonate-chemistry calculation (TA 2300 µmol/kg, S 35, SST ~19.6 °C, surface fCO2 573 µatm from Jiang et al. 2023), scaled by ~1.08 so it reproduces Jiang's published 1750 (3.6), 2010 (3.0), SSP1-1.9 (2.9) and SSP5-8.5 (1.6) values. The 2.50 line corresponds to surface fCO2 ~520 µatm, i.e. atmospheric CO2 ~540-560 ppm. Replace with the Jiang et al. supplementary Table S7/S8 value if someone can open it.

OCEAN ACIDIFICATION BOUNDARY UNCERTAINTY: PHC 2026 uses pre-industrial 3.57, boundary 2.86, 2024 value 2.85 ± 0.01. Findlay et al. 2025 used pre-industrial 3.51 ± 0.065 (range 3.44-3.57), boundary 2.80 ± 0.05, and present-day 2.90 ± 0.06, i.e. 'inside the uncertainty range' rather than clearly past it. The global mean hides that over 40% of the surface ocean and up to 60% of the top 200 m had already crossed the 20% line by 2020.

SEA LEVEL: the brief's factorId is 'sea_level' (cm since 1993) but the site code currently has 'sea_level_rate' (mm/yr, 4.75 for 2012-2025). Projections and thresholds here are in cm relative to 1995-2014 (IPCC baseline); add about 3 cm to compare with the January 1993 start of the WMO 11 cm figure. The 50 cm and 1 m lines are this pass's choice, not published thresholds.

PERMAFROST UNIT MISMATCH: the card shows the share of monitored sites at a record high (62.5% = 15 of 24, BAMS State of the Climate in 2025). That indicator has no 2100 projection. Thresholds and exceedance here are in a different unit (% of near-surface permafrost volume lost), flagged with a 'unit' key. The abrupt-thaw tipping point (~1.5 °C, Armstrong McKay 2022; GTPR 2025) is covered by the 1.5 °C warming threshold. The BAMS 15-of-24 figure could not be re-verified (journals.ametsoc.org returns 403).

AMOC DISAGREEMENT: IPCC AR6 (2021) gives medium confidence of no abrupt collapse before 2100 (earlier reports said 'very unlikely', <10%). Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen 2023 (early-warning statistics) estimate collapse around mid-century under current emissions; a 2026 review gives their mean tipping year as 2065 (95% range 2037-2109). Smolders et al. 2024 preprint: collapse 2037-2064 (10-90%), 59 ± 17% before 2050. van Westen et al. 2024 preprint (CESM): >50% chance of tipping this century under a middle-of-the-road scenario, >90% under high emissions. Drijfhout et al. 2025 (CMIP6 runs extended past 2100): deep-convection collapse mid-century, northern shutdown by 2300 in 25% (SSP1-2.6), 37% (SSP2-4.5) and 70% (SSP5-8.5) of runs, with shutdown happening after 2100. Cini et al. (EGU 2026 abstract, intermediate-complexity model, SSP5-8.5): below 1% by 2100, ~20% by 2150, ~95% by 2200. Baker et al. 2025 (Nature): a weak, shallow AMOC persists even under extremes. Portmann et al. 2026: 51 ± 8% weakening by 2100 under SSP2-4.5; Bonan et al. 2025: 18-43%. Observations: RAPID shows ~4 Sv decline 2004-2012 then partial recovery; air-sea heat-flux reconstructions show no decline 1963-2017 (Terhaar et al. 2025). Drijfhout & Sanchez-Franks (arXiv, Nov 2026) argue models may now be too unstable. Dijkstra et al. 2026 (WIREs, 22 authors) conclude the present-day AMOC is in a multi-stable regime and an eventual collapse may already be unavoidable even under SSP2-4.5 without deep cuts. Summary: most experts now see a 21st-century tipping point as plausible; a fully collapsed state by 2100 remains less likely than not. A judged ~0.3 chance that a tipping point is passed before 2100 (committing to later collapse) is reasonable but is not entered as an exceedance because it has no Sv value.
AMOC Sv mapping: Portmann and Bonan publish percentage weakening, not Sv at 26°N. Applying those percentages to the RAPID 17.1 Sv mean is illustrative only.

ARCTIC: Jahn 2018 uses one model (CESM) and calls its results a lower bound on ice loss because of model biases. AR6 says there is no tipping point for summer sea-ice loss: ice would return if temperatures fell. WMO gives the 2025 minimum as 4.74 ± 0.35 million km² (multi-dataset); NSIDC via NASA gives 4.6 for both 2025 and 2026 (tied 10th lowest).

BIODIVERSITY: LPR 2026 figures (73.2%, 1970-2022, 35,803 populations, 5,790 species) were read via Our World in Data; realm and regional splits (freshwater 85%, terrestrial 69%, marine 59%; Latin America & Caribbean 95%, Africa 80%, Asia-Pacific 49%, North America 28%, Europe & Central Asia 23%) only via a secondary summary (WWF and IISD pages return 403). The 80%/90% thresholds and their probabilities are judgment.

PLANETARY BOUNDARIES: all thresholds and exceedances are judged. Judged chance that at least seven remain crossed in 2100: ~0.9 (CO2 stays above 350 ppm in every SSP; ocean acidification stays past its line in all but the lowest path).

CLIMATE VULNERABILITY (ND-GAIN): explainer only, no 2100 thresholds. Values read from the ND-GAIN 2026 release CSV already downloaded to scratchpad/raw/dl_ndgain (2024 column, 190 countries): lowest Norway 0.263, highest Mauritania 0.655, Somalia and Chad 0.638. Site values match. The score rises with vulnerability. Most countries' scores fell slowly 1995-2024 (e.g. India 0.551 to 0.475), because adaptive capacity improved, not because hazards shrank.

WATER STRESS (Aqueduct 4.0): explainer plus 2050 country values from the workbook already in scratchpad/raw/dl_aq (country_future, bws, total-demand weight). Counting countries scored 'extremely high' gives 25 at baseline and 29 in 2050 under business-as-usual (DERIVED count). WRI's article: 25 countries with a quarter of the world's population face extremely high stress; ~4 billion people face high stress at least one month a year; by 2050 about 1 billion more people with extremely high stress, demand up 20-25%, 100% of Middle East and North Africa population extremely stressed, 31% of global GDP exposed. Aqueduct cautions: indicators are not validated, inter-basin transfers are not modelled. Aqueduct gives scenario values, not probabilities, so no exceedance is given.

SOURCE ACCESS: unep.org, wwf, iisd, journals.ametsoc.org and pnas.org returned 403. IPCC text was read from official-copy mirrors (energy.gov SPM, ITLOS-hosted Chapter 9). The Planetary Health Check 2026 PDF (27.8 MB) was downloaded with curl to scratchpad/raw/climate/phc2026.pdf because it exceeded the fetch tool's size limit.
All exceedance values describe the baseline trajectory without any special SI effect; the site's 'with SI' column should adjust them separately.
